blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the main causes of poverty - including unemployment, low wages, illness and age - and trace how they work through households and whole towns.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: The main causes and their shape
blocks.text: The causes work on income or on need. On the income side sit unemployment and low pay: a household whose earners cannot find work has no wage to live on, and low pay holds a household near the poverty line even in work, often because weak education and skills limit what a worker can command. On the need side sit large households with many dependants, where one wage must feed many, so income per person is low even where the wage is not; illness and disability, which cut earnings and raise spending at once; and old age without a pension. Two causes reach whole regions: drought that destroys harvests where families farm to eat, and distance from jobs, as in Namibia's sparsely settled north, where the nearest employer may be far away. The causes also tend to compound across generations: low income limits the schooling a household can afford, and weak schooling limits the next generation's pay.

blocks.heading: One closure traced through a town
blocks.text: Trace a cause through a town. A garment workshop in Oshakati closes, and its 120 workers lose their monthly wage - that is the starting point. Because each wage of about N$3 600 was the main income of a household, spending on food, rent and transport is cut back at once; the town's shops lose about 120 x N$3 600 = N$432 000 of sales a month. This causes the shops to take on fewer workers and some to close, so poverty spreads to households whose earners never worked for the garment firm. Therefore one closure can create more of its own kind: joblessness lowers spending, and lower spending takes away more jobs. In Vietnam, garment towns that lost orders saw the same spread, with poverty rising furthest among the least skilled workers.

blocks.heading: Illness and age as causes of poverty
blocks.text:
Two causes deserve a closer look, because each works on income and on need at the same time.

Illness: when an earner falls seriously ill, the household loses wages if the earner cannot work, or earns less where hours are cut, and in a job without sick pay the wage stops at once. At the same time spending rises: medicine, transport to a clinic, and a relative's time spent caring rather than working. Suppose a taxi driver in Rundu earning N$4 000 a month is too ill to work for three months: the household loses 3 x N$4 000 = N$12 000 of income and pays for treatment besides. Where healthcare is not free, savings may be used up or livestock sold, so the household can stay poorer even after recovery.

Age: older people who can no longer work lose their wage, and without a pension or savings they may fall into poverty; Namibia pays an old-age pension to older residents for this reason. At the other end of life, young people may struggle to find a first job because they lack experience, and youth unemployment tends to be higher than adult unemployment. A household with many children or elderly relatives also has more people to support from each wage, so income per person falls.
